commitResults.messageBody:
The test suite checks that the app behaves correctly for the inputs it
is handed. It says nothing about the assumptions the code relies on in
between, so a broken assumption surfaces as wrong output somewhere
downstream rather than as a failure at the point that actually broke.

Add assert statements at the seven places where an assumption has to
hold for the surrounding code to make sense. Two are worth calling out.
Command.toIndex returns an index that every subclass immediately hands
to tasks.get, so an off-by-one would quietly act on the wrong task
instead of failing. Ui.flush must leave its buffer empty, because
leftover text would be prepended to the next reply and show up in the
GUI as an answer to a different question.

These document internal assumptions rather than validate user input,
which stays on exceptions. An assertion firing always means the code
is wrong, never that the user typed something unusual.

Java disables assertions at runtime by default, so enable them with -ea
on the test and run tasks. Without that none of these would ever
execute, and the increment would be decorative.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams for task list queries
commitResults.messageBody:
findOn, find and toSaveFormat each built their result the same way:
declare an empty list, walk every task, add the ones that qualify,
return the list. The loop scaffolding took up more room than the rule
being applied, which was a single line buried in the middle of each.

Express all three as stream pipelines so the rule reads directly off
the code, which also removes sixteen lines. The returned lists are now
unmodifiable, and that suits every caller, since all three only read
what they are given.

Storage.load keeps its indexed loop on purpose. It needs the line
number for its warnings, catches a checked exception per line, and
produces two results rather than one. A stream there would be longer
and harder to follow than the loop it replaced, so streams are used
where they clarify and left out where they would not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix code quality issues raised in review
commitResults.messageBody:
Peer review of the iP pull request raised several issues, two of them
substantive enough to change the design rather than just the wording.

Task was a concrete class that nothing ever instantiated directly. A
bare Task carries no type letter, so it would serialise to a record
that Storage cannot read back. Making it abstract turns that from
something merely unused into something the compiler rules out.

Ui.showTaskList carried its own copy of the numbering loop that
showNumbered already had, because one took a TaskList and the other a
List. TaskList.asList now returns an unmodifiable view so both share a
single implementation. The duplication was what got reported, but the
better outcome is that the user interface no longer receives a list it
is able to modify.

The rest are smaller: American spelling in five places as the coding
standard requires, correct singular in "1 task in the list", and
splitting a test that bundled three assertions so a failure in the
first no longer hides the other two.

Raised by xian-zhe and herohelennn1010 on #528.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Share task type letters with storage
commitResults.messageBody:
The letters T, D and E appeared in two places: once in each task's
toSaveFormat, and again in the switch in Storage that reads records
back. Nothing tied the two sides together, so changing a letter in one
place would still compile, then fail at load time by reporting the
affected lines as an unknown task type, well away from the edit that
caused it.

Give each subclass a TYPE_LETTER constant and have Storage switch on
those constants instead of repeating the literals. The writing and
reading sides can no longer drift apart, because a rename now updates
both by construction.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
A-Assertions: use assertions to document key assumptions
A-CodeQuality: address review feedback and remove duplication
A-Streams: use streams for task list queries

Tasks could only be found by the words in their description, so anything
that cut across descriptions, such as everything for one module or
everything worth doing when bored, had no way to be grouped.

Let a task carry any number of labels, added and removed one at a time
with tag and untag. Tags are held in an insertion-ordered set, so
tagging twice is a no-op rather than an error and tags appear in the
order they were added. A leading hash is optional and case is folded, so
#Fun, fun and #fun are one tag. find now searches tags as well as
descriptions, since a label nothing can look up is not worth storing.

The save format needed care. Records had an exact field count per type,
so tags go in one optional trailing field and the count became a choice
of two. A task with no tags writes no field at all, which leaves its
record byte for byte what it was before, and task lists saved before
tagging existed load unchanged.

Tags typed by the user are validated to letters, digits, hyphens and
underscores, which also guarantees they cannot contain the separator the
save format relies on. Tags read back from file are taken as they are
found, because the field has already been split on that separator and a
label the app did not write itself does no harm.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
C-Tagging: tag tasks with labels such as #fun
